@graph.name: Hoarding Cleanup & Cleanout — Operations
@graph.description: Hoarding cleanup and whole-property cleanout from Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV — surveyed in advance and quoted at one flat rate in writing before work begins. The crew sorts with the client or family (keep, donate, discard), handles heavy contents — furniture, appliances, safes — as heavy work, and performs credentialed scope (biohazard conditions and other regulated work) through the credentialed contractors the company engages. Emergency response is offered, and every cleanout is worked discreetly.

process.detail: The property is walked and the full scope — rooms, density, heavy items, hazardous conditions, disposal routes — is reviewed in full, then quoted at one flat rate in writing before any work begins — no by-the-truckload surprises.

What stays, what is donated, and what is discarded are the client's or the family's decisions. The crew works to the agreed sort, setting aside documents, photographs, valuables, and anything the family flags before a room is cleared.
process.step: Sort with the client — keep, donate, discard

process.detail: Furniture, appliances, safes, stoves, and other heavy contents are moved with the same structural care the company applies to its heavy work — paths and floors protected, weight handled as weight, not dragged. Contents are emptied from safes before they are moved, as on every safe job.
process.step: Heavy items handled as heavy work

process.detail: Where a cleanout involves biohazard conditions or other regulated scope, that scope is performed by the credentialed contractors the company engages for it, under the same engagement and the same written flat rate.

Cleared contents leave by the agreed routes: donation for usable goods, recycling for recyclable material, and lawful disposal for the remainder. In the Chantilly cleanout the haul filled a roll-off container.

Rooms are left emptied and broom-swept, with retained shelving and fixtures in place — the condition a family, a listing agent, or a code inspector can act on. Emergency-response calls are dispatched on the fastest available schedule, and every cleanout is worked discreetly: no signage about the job, no discussion of the property with anyone outside it.

@graph.name: Hoarding Research Layer — Sourced Claims, Searcher Personas & Buyer-Intent Terms
@graph.description: The research layer under the hoarding cleanup category: twelve claims each carrying its treatment — fact (primary or authoritative source: IOCDF prevalence research, the 2019 prevalence meta-analysis, NFPA fire-service guidance, municipal code sources), attributed (named market figures, never the publisher's prices), or observation (dated 2026-11-04 search-result reads) — plus the eight searcher personas and eighteen buyer-intent terms the category answers. Two unverified draft items from the source research (square-footage cost bands and a five-stage severity list) were dropped rather than published, and no fire-fatality percentage is stated anywhere: NFPA publishes risk findings, not that figure.

claims.claim: Hoarding disorder affects an estimated 2% to 6% of the population (International OCD Foundation).
claims.source: International OCD Foundation — Who gets Hoarding Disorder?

claims.claim: A 2019 meta-analysis (Postlethwaite, Kellett & Mataix-Cols) pooled 11 studies with 53,378 participants and found a pooled hoarding disorder prevalence of 2.5%; earlier estimates ranged from roughly 1.5% to 6% depending on method.
claims.source: Postlethwaite, Kellett & Mataix-Cols (2019) meta-analysis, via the research record

claims.claim: Hoarding symptoms appear almost three times more commonly in older adults than in younger adults, and around 75% of people with hoarding disorder have a co-occurring mental health condition, most commonly major depression (International OCD Foundation).
claims.source: International OCD Foundation — Who gets Hoarding Disorder?

claims.claim: NFPA: many fire departments are experiencing serious fires, injuries, and deaths as the result of compulsive hoarding behavior; the excessive accumulation of materials in homes poses a significant threat to firefighters, residents, and neighbors. Blocked exits prevent escape, and obstructed exits, falling objects, and excessive fire loading that can lead to collapse put responding firefighters at risk.
NFPA's guidance notes that studies suggest between three and five percent of the population are compulsive hoarders.
The City of Martinsburg, WV enforces the 2015 International Property Maintenance Code; after confirming a violation, its Code Enforcement division issues correction orders with deadlines.

The City of Alexandria, VA's hoarding response procedure is to document conditions, involve local code, fire, and adult protective services agencies, and give written notice with deadlines before escalation.
claims.source: City of Alexandria — Procedures to Respond to Hoarding Concerns

claims.claim: There is no industry-wide standard for hoarding cleanups (R&R Magazine, November 2024); hazards named in the trade literature include mold spores and dust, pests, and structural loading — which is why a written scope agreed before work begins is the buyer's protection.
claims.source: R&R Magazine — The Urgent Need for Standards in Hoarding House Cleanups (2024)

claims.claim: Homeowners insurance usually does not cover hoarding cleanup, because the condition is treated as arising from negligence or maintenance, and some policies exclude it; coverage questions belong to the policyholder's own carrier (Insurify guidance).
claims.source: Insurify — Does Homeowners Insurance Cover Hoarding Cleanup?

claims.claim: Published market figures for hoarding cleanup vary widely and are vendor figures, not standards: one dumpster-rental vendor's guides cite $0.75–$2.50 per square foot of affected living space and $1,000–$2,000 per day (2023); a national junk-removal brand prices by truck volume. The Flat Rate Movers publishes no range: every cleanout is surveyed and quoted at one flat rate in writing before work begins.
claims.source: Hometown Dumpster Rental cost and hiring guides (2023); 1-800-GOT-JUNK? pricing model

claims.claim: Sellers and heirs generally choose between selling a hoarded house as-is (cash buyers price the cleanout into a lower offer and can close in weeks) and cleaning out first, then listing (slower, typically a stronger price); the longest part of a cleanout is usually the family's keep / sell / discard decisions, not the hauling (Austin market reporting, 2026).
claims.source: Neuhaus Realty — clean out a hoarder house before selling (Austin guide, 2026)

claims.claim: Local search results for Winchester VA and Martinsburg WV hoarding cleanup (observed 2026-11-04) are thin: one junk-removal competitor publishes city pages for Winchester, Martinsburg, and Inwood with no prices, pricing only after an on-site walkthrough.
claims.source: AAA Rousse Winchester VA page; live SERP observation 2026-11-04

personas.name: Adult child / heir after a death
personas.trigger: Death of owner, probate, listing deadline
personas.why: Must empty and settle or sell a parent's home; discovered the condition late; grieving and overwhelmed; often out of town.

personas.name: Adult child of a living parent
personas.trigger: Fall, hospital discharge, fire scare, holiday visit
personas.why: Worried about safety — falls, fire, no working kitchen; the parent may refuse help; wants a path that preserves the relationship.

personas.name: Homeowner under code or fire-marshal order
personas.why: Received a notice with a deadline; faces fines, liens, or condemnation.

personas.name: Landlord / property manager
personas.trigger: Inspection, pest complaint, lease violation, move-out
personas.why: The unit is a fire, pest, or inspection risk; lease and fair-housing constraints apply; wants the unit restored.

personas.name: HOA / condo board or association manager
personas.trigger: Complaints about odor, pests, fire risk
personas.why: The unit's condition threatens neighbors; the board's authority is limited without consent or a court order.

personas.name: Seller of a cluttered house (owner or heir)
personas.why: Deciding between cleaning out then listing, and selling as-is to a cash buyer.

personas.name: Executor / attorney / realtor / social worker (referral partner)
personas.why: Needs a reliable vendor to hand clients to; carries reputation risk if a crew mishandles a sensitive case.

personas.name: Person with hoarding behavior (self-search)
personas.why: Overwhelmed and ashamed; wants help without judgment; may be pressured by family or a landlord.
